tracks.label: Opening
tracks.text: Chapter 1. Energy, Power and the Global Picture. Right now Earth is intercepting sunlight at a rate of about 174,000 terawatts. That figure is a short calculation: the solar irradiance above the atmosphere, about 1,361 watts per square meter, times the area of Earth’s disk, π(6,371 km)². Humanity’s total energy supply in 2025 was just over 600 exajoules, which averages to about 19 terawatts, so less than an hour of sunlight carries as much energy as civilization uses in a year. Yet solar power supplied only about 1.3 percent of world energy in 2024 on the accounting the Energy Institute now uses, and roughly 3 percent on the substitution method it used through its 2024 edition. Same panels, same kilowatt-hours, a factor of more than two. Seeing why takes units, an accounting framework and a way to draw the flows. This chapter sets up the quantitative language of the whole book. Section 1.1 separates energy from power and builds fluency in the units that energy statistics use, from the joule and kilowatt-hour to the exajoule and the quad, with a ladder of power levels for order-of-magnitude checks. Section 1.2 follows energy from primary sources through conversion to final and useful energy, starts the running example of one kilowatt-hour, and explains the three conventions for counting electricity from sources that burn no fuel. Section 1.3 teaches you to read and check Sankey diagrams, using the Lawrence Livermore chart of US energy flows. Later chapters supply the physics behind each loss you meet here: thermodynamic limits in Chapter 2, grid losses in Chapter 3, plant heat rates in Chapter 4 and capacity factors in Chapter 5.

tracks.label: 1.1 Energy and power: units and scales
tracks.text: Section 1 point 1. Energy and power: units and scales. Two quantities run through this whole book, and most mistakes in energy arguments come from swapping them. Energy is the capacity to do work or deliver heat; its SI unit is the joule (J), the work done by a force of one newton acting through one meter. Power is the rate at which energy is converted or transferred; its SI unit is the watt (W), and 1 W = 1 J/s. Energy is a stock and power is a flow. A power plant’s capacity is a power, in megawatts (MW); what it sells is energy, in megawatt-hours (MWh). A 500 MW combined-cycle gas plant, one of this book’s two reference plants, running at full output for one hour delivers 500 MW times 1 h = 500 MWh. The same plant held in reserve all year still has 500 MW of capacity and sells nothing. The kilowatt-hour (kWh) is the energy of one kilowatt sustained for one hour: 1 kWh = 1,000 J/s times 3,600 s = 3.6 times 10⁶ J = 3.6 MJ, exactly. It is the unit on an electricity bill, and one kilowatt-hour is the running example we will follow from fuel to socket through the rest of the book. To feel its size, lift a 1,000 kg car with it: h = E/(mg) = 3.6 times 10⁶ J / (1,000 kg times 9.81 m/s²) = 367 m. Or heat water: at 4,186 J/(kg·K), 1 kWh warms 3.6 times 10⁶ J / (4,186 J/(kg·K) times 80 K) = 10.7 kg of water from 20 degrees Celsius to 100 degrees Celsius. A food Calorie is a kilocalorie, 4,186.8 J, so a 2,000 kcal daily diet supplies 8.37 MJ, or 2.33 kWh. Spread over 86,400 s, that is 97 W: a person runs on roughly the power of an old incandescent bulb. Energy statistics span so many orders of magnitude that each community keeps its own units. SI prefixes step by factors of 1,000: kilo (10³), mega (10⁶), giga (10⁹), tera (10¹²), peta (10¹⁵) and exa (10¹⁸). Electricity statistics use kWh, MWh, GWh and TWh, where 1 TWh = 10⁹ kWh = 3.6 PJ. Global statistics use the exajoule (EJ): 1 EJ = 10¹⁸ J / (3.6 times 10¹⁵ J/TWh) = 277.8 TWh. US agencies use the British thermal unit, defined as 1,055.056 J (the International Table Btu), and the quad, 10¹⁵ Btu = 1.055 times 10¹⁸ J = 1.055 EJ. One quad is therefore 293.1 TWh. Write each conversion as a fraction equal to one, such as (1.055 EJ / 1 quad), and cancel the units on paper before you touch a calculator. Order-of-magnitude reasoning comes before precision, so carry a ladder of power levels in your head (Figure 1.1). A phone charger draws about 20 W. A household that uses 10,000 kWh of electricity a year averages 10,000 kWh / 8,760 h = 1.14 kW. A large modern offshore wind turbine is rated at around 15 MW, a combined-cycle gas plant at several hundred megawatts. The world’s total energy supply in 2025, just over 600 EJ according to the Energy Institute’s 2026 Statistical Review, averages 600 times 10¹⁸ J / 3.154 times 10⁷ s = 19 TW. Above all of these sits the Sun. Measured above the atmosphere, sunlight delivers about 1,361 W/m²; over Earth’s cross-section, π(6.371 times 10⁶ m)² = 1.275 times 10¹⁴ m², that is 1.74 times 10¹⁷ W. From charger to sunlight spans 16 orders of magnitude. Dividing an annual energy total by the seconds or hours in a year converts it into an average power, and this one step does a great deal of work in this book. The United States consumed 94.2 quads of primary energy in 2024, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA). That is 99.4 EJ, an average of 3.14 TW over the 366 days of a leap year (worked below). With about 340 million residents, that comes to roughly 9 kW per person, against about 2.3 kW for the world, where 19 TW is shared among some 8.2 billion people. The same arithmetic, run the other way, defines the capacity factor of Chapter 5: a 200 MW wind farm, our second reference plant, that produced 613,200 MWh in a year averaged 613,200 MWh / 8,760 h = 70 MW, or 35 percent of its rating. A common misconception: “Our solar panels made 6 kW today.” In fact, A day’s output is energy, in kWh; kW describes how fast the panels produce at an instant, or their rated peak. A 6 kW array might produce 30 kWh on a sunny day, and “6 kW per day” mixes a rate with a time. The reverse error, “kilowatts per hour,” is a real unit (a ramp rate, which matters for power plants in Chapter 7) but is almost never what the speaker meant.

tracks.label: 1.2 Primary energy and final use
tracks.text: Section 1 point 2. Primary energy and final use. Energy statistics follow energy through a chain of forms, and every link loses something. Primary energy is energy as first extracted or captured from nature: crude oil, coal and natural gas as they leave the ground, the heat released in a reactor, the electricity from a wind turbine or a hydro dam. Refineries and power plants convert it into secondary energy carriers such as gasoline, electricity, district heat or hydrogen. Final energy is what end users buy and meter: liters at the pump, kWh at the meter, cubic meters of gas at the boiler. End-use devices turn final energy into useful energy (heat in a room, torque at a wheel, light), which provides an energy service such as a warm room or a kilometer traveled. The International Energy Agency (IEA) reports national energy at the first and third of these stages, as total energy supply and total final consumption. Follow one kilowatt-hour back from a socket. Suppose it came from a combined-cycle gas plant that converts 55 percent of the fuel’s heat into electricity (Chapter 2 explains how two cycles in series reach this), and that 5 percent of the electricity sent out is lost in transmission and distribution (Section 1.3 and Chapter 3). The plant must send out 1 kWh / 0.95 = 1.053 kWh and burn 1.053 kWh / 0.55 = 1.91 kWh of gas, or 6.89 MJ. Only 52 percent of the primary energy reaches the socket. What happens next depends on the device. An electric motor at 90 percent efficiency turns the kWh into 0.9 kWh of shaft work, while a heat pump with a coefficient of performance of 3 delivers 3 kWh of heat. Useful energy can exceed final energy because the heat pump moves heat drawn from outdoor air; the second law, in Chapter 2, sets how much. For fuels, primary energy is the heat released by burning them, but even that needs a convention. The higher heating value (gross calorific value) includes the latent heat recovered if the water vapor in the exhaust condenses; the lower heating value (net calorific value) excludes it. For natural gas the two differ by about 10 percent. The IEA and most international statistics use net values, while the EIA uses gross values. International statistics also report energy in tonnes of oil equivalent, defined as 10⁷ kcal = 41.868 GJ, so 1 Mtoe = 41.868 PJ = 11.63 TWh. Chapter 4 returns to heating values when we compute a plant’s fuel cost from its heat rate; for now, note which basis any efficiency or heat rate you read is quoted on. The hard problem is electricity from sources that burn nothing. There is no fuel to weigh, so a convention must decide what counts as primary energy, and three are in use. The physical energy content method, used by the IEA and Eurostat, takes the first energy form downstream for which more than one use is practical. For hydro, wind and solar photovoltaics that is electricity, so 1 kWh counts as 3.6 MJ. For nuclear and geothermal it is heat, estimated by assuming conversion efficiencies of 33 percent and 10 percent. The direct equivalent method, used in IPCC assessments, counts every non-combustible source, nuclear included, at its electricity output. The substitution method counts the fuel a typical thermal plant would have burned to make the same electricity: at an assumed 40 percent efficiency, 1 kWh of wind becomes 3.6 MJ / 0.40 = 9.0 MJ (Figure 1.2). The choice moves headline numbers. The Energy Institute’s Statistical Review, one of the most quoted global datasets, used the substitution method through its 2024 edition, which reported 620 EJ of primary energy for 2023. Its 2025 edition switched to the physical energy content method, in line with the IEA and EIA, and reported 2024 wind and solar output of 9.04 EJ and 7.72 EJ. Together that is 16.8 EJ, or 4,660 TWh, about 2.8 percent of a world total of roughly 590 EJ. Count the same electricity by substitution at 40 percent and it becomes 16.8 EJ / 0.40 = 41.9 EJ, about 6.8 percent of a correspondingly larger total. Nothing physical changed. The substitution method estimates how much fossil fuel these sources stand in for; the physical content method records the energy that entered the economy. Chapter 8 shows why the difference grows as transport and heat electrify. US statistics went through the same change. Beginning with its September 2023 Monthly Energy Review, the EIA counts electricity from wind, solar and hydro at its heat content, 3,412 Btu per kWh, which is simply 3.6 MJ expressed in Btu. Before that it used fossil fuel equivalence, valuing each renewable kWh at the heat rate of fossil-fuel plants, a substitution method. Nuclear electricity is still counted as reactor heat, through the fleet’s heat rate, so the US convention now resembles the physical energy content method. The EIA’s documentation also describes a third option, incident energy, which would count the sunlight striking a panel or the wind passing a rotor. Because the Lawrence Livermore flow charts in Section 1.3 are built from EIA data, this choice sits inside every band of those diagrams. A common misconception: “Wind and solar are under 3 percent of world energy, so they hardly matter to the energy system.” In fact, The figure depends on the stage and the method. On the physical content method, wind and solar were about 2.8 percent of world primary energy in 2024; by substitution they would be about 7 percent. Their share of electricity generation, about 15 percent in 2024, is much higher than either, because electricity is the stage at which they enter the system. Always ask which stage (primary, final or electricity) and which method a percentage uses.

tracks.label: 1.3 Reading energy flow (Sankey) diagrams
tracks.text: Section 1 point 3. Reading energy flow (Sankey) diagrams. In 1898 the engineer Matthew Henry Phineas Riall Sankey published a diagram of a steam engine in which the width of each arrow was proportional to the heat flowing through it; the broad band of heat entering the boiler narrowed to a thin band of useful work, with the rest peeling off as losses. Diagrams of this kind now carry his name. Earlier flow maps existed, most famously Charles Joseph Minard’s 1869 chart of Napoleon’s army in Russia, but Sankey made the form a tool of energy engineering. A Sankey diagram follows three rules. Band width is proportional to quantity. All bands share one unit. And flows are conserved at every node, so what enters a box equals what leaves it plus any change in storage. The best-known energy Sankey diagram is the chart of US energy flows that Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) publishes from EIA data. Read it from left to right. Primary sources sit in a column on the left: solar, nuclear, hydro, wind, geothermal, natural gas, coal, biomass and petroleum. Some flows run to a box for electricity generation; the rest go straight to the four end-use sectors, residential, commercial, industrial and transportation, which also receive electricity. On the right, every sector splits into two sinks: energy services, the estimated useful energy, and rejected energy, heat released to the environment. The units are quads, and the chart for 2023 totals 93.6 quads (Figure 1.3). The 2023 chart can be checked with arithmetic. Of 93.6 quads, 61.5 appear as rejected energy and 32.1 as energy services, and 61.5 + 32.1 = 93.6, so the diagram closes. Electricity generation takes in about 32 quads of primary energy (we use 32.1 below). The four sectors receive 11.3 (residential), 9.3 (commercial), 26.1 (industrial) and 28.0 (transportation) quads, 74.7 quads in all, electricity included. Fuel used directly in the sectors is 93.6 minus 32.1 = 61.5 quads, so the electricity delivered must be 74.7 minus 61.5 = 13.2 quads, about 3,870 TWh, and 32.1 minus 13.2 = 18.9 quads leave the power sector as rejected energy. About 41 percent of the primary energy entering US power plants in 2023 reached customers as electricity. Two cautions apply to the right-hand side. Rejected energy is not all waste that better engineering could recover: much of it is the heat that any heat engine must reject to its cold reservoir, a limit Chapter 2 derives from the second law. And energy services are not measured. LLNL estimates them by applying an assumed end-use efficiency to each sector, lowest for transportation, where most fuel burns in combustion engines, so the 32.1 quads of services is a model result. Some losses are also smaller than intuition suggests. The EIA estimates that transmission and distribution losses average about 5 percent of the electricity moved through the US grid, while the US thermal fleet as a whole loses more than half of its fuel’s energy as heat. Because LLNL builds its chart from EIA statistics, the accounting method of Section 1.2 sits inside every band. The chart for 2022, as first published, totals 100.3 quads; the chart for 2023 totals 93.6. US energy use did not fall 7 percent in a year. Most of the gap reflects the EIA’s switch to the captured energy approach. A rough estimate shows the size: the United States generated on the order of 900 TWh from wind, solar and hydro, and re-counting that electricity at 3,412 Btu/kWh instead of a fossil-plant heat rate of roughly 9,500 Btu/kWh removes 9 times 10¹¹ kWh times 6,100 Btu/kWh about 5.5 times 10¹⁵ Btu, or about 5.5 quads, mostly from the power sector’s rejected energy. Compare Sankey diagrams across years or countries only after checking that they share an accounting basis. Sankey diagrams work at every scale, from one engine to the planet. Cullen and Allwood drew a global diagram for 2005 that follows energy from fuels through conversion devices, such as engines, furnaces and electric motors, to final services such as transport, heating and illumination. To build one for a country, as this chapter’s challenge asks, start from an energy balance table: the IEA’s World Energy Balances or a national agency’s. Fix one year, one unit and one accounting method. Draw the nodes (primary sources, transformation, end-use sectors), size each band from the table, and check that every node closes to within the table’s statistical difference, the line in an energy balance that records what the data cannot reconcile. A common misconception: “Two-thirds of America’s energy is wasted, so better efficiency could cut energy use by two-thirds.” In fact, Much of the rejected energy is heat that the second law requires every heat engine to reject, and the services estimate rests on assumed efficiencies. Large savings come mainly from changing conversion technology, for example replacing combustion engines and boilers with electric motors and heat pumps, or thermal generation with wind and solar, which also changes how the chart is drawn (Section 1.2).
